source.title_on_document: Measuring and mitigating persona distortions from AI writing assistance

supplement.where: https://github.com/paul-rottger/ai-distortion (p. 16, Data and Code Availability Statement). The saved PDF ends with references on p. 20 and contains no SI.
supplement.holds: SI:1.4 attrition; SI:2.4 exact reader-rating questions; SI:5.6 main regression specifications/outputs; SI:5.7-5.8 model/input variants; SI:5.9 per-attribute SD/entropy homogenization analyses; SI:7.3 disclaimer regressions; SI:8.4 mitigation rating regressions and SI:8.5 writer-preference regressions; SI:9.4 trust and SI:10.4 persuasion regressions. The main PDF does not give the numeric SEs/CIs or complete arm statistics needed for the coded originality/quality/dispersion effects (pp. 4, 12-15).

paper_design_summary: UK adults on Prolific first wrote political opinion paragraphs and then edited AI-generated versions; separate blinded readers rated the writing and inferred writer characteristics. Five studies covered persona distortions, randomized writer disclaimers, AI mitigation configurations in randomized within-writer order, and reader trust and persuasion. Originality and writing-quality ratings bear on with_ai and dispersion of perceptions bears on across_people, but the main AI-versus-unaided writing comparison used a fixed order.

studies.label: Study 1: Main writing and persona-perception study

assignment.what_was_assigned: For the AI-versus-unaided comparisons recorded here, all writers first composed their own text and then received and edited AI text; assistance versus no assistance and its order were not randomized. Political propositions, AI models, and input formats were randomly assigned/paired, including rewrite versus improve for paragraph input. Those randomized AI-configuration components must not be mistaken for random assignment of the pooled AI-versus-unaided contrast. Separate readers were randomly assigned paragraphs to rate.
assignment.quote: after writers had composed their own paragraph and edited the AI-generated version to their satisfaction
assignment.locator: p. 3, Figure 1 and Section 2; p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 12, Sections 4.4 and 4.6
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/6exf2 (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: Own paragraph (unaided reference)
arms.description: Writers first compose their own paragraph. Same writer sample as the AI condition; no independent no-AI group (p. 3, Figure 1). Arm-specific distinct writer counts after the analysis restriction are not stated.

arms.name: AI-assisted paragraph (including writer edits)
arms.description: AI drafts from stance, bullets, or the existing paragraph and the writer may edit it. Main comparison includes edits and excludes cases where AI text was strictly dispreferred (pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and Section 2.2).

participants.exclusions: Initial assignment and attrition counts are not supplied; attrition is referred to absent SI:1.4 (p. 11). The main perception analysis removes 708 of 4,503 writer-proposition cases (15.7%) where AI text was strictly dispreferred and includes writer edits (p. 4, Section 2.2). These are output-pair exclusions, not 708 excluded people. The number of distinct writers remaining for each restricted outcome is not stated.
participants.who: Adults aged 18+ recruited on Prolific in the UK. The analyzed writer study sample is reported as 1,501 completers; writers were sampled to match UK census age, gender, and race. An additional 10,017 readers rated the writing; those raters are not added to the writer sample size (p. 11, Section 4.1).
participants.quote: Study 1 was completed by 1,501 writers and 10,017 readers

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o)
ai_tool.how_used: Structured drafting from the writer's stance rating or bullet points, or rewriting/improving the writer's own paragraph, followed by writer editing. Model/input pairings are randomized within writers in Studies 1 and 2. This is human use and editing of AI assistance, not an AI-only versus human-only output comparison. Models are accessed through OpenRouter (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.3-4.5).

task.description: Write political opinion paragraphs on three propositions sampled from a pool of 100. Writers first give a 0-100 stance rating, at least two explanatory bullet points, and their own paragraph of at least 100 words; they then edit an AI-generated paragraph until it reflects their opinion. AI paragraphs based on stance/bullets are requested at 100-150 words; paragraph-input conditions rewrite or improve the existing paragraph without changing its length (pp. 3, 11-12, Sections 2, 4.2, 4.4-4.5).

outcomes.name: Dispersion of perceived writer confidence across paragraphs
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The main text gives confidence as its numeric example of homogenization. SDs summarize perceptions across paragraphs; they are not the SDs for a creativity mean-difference effect. No confidence-specific uncertainty is printed (p. 4, Section 2.2).

contrasts.reported: Perceived writer confidence: human-written paragraphs 24.1 SD versus AI-assisted paragraphs 20.5 SD. No attribute-specific p-value, CI, SE, or final analysis count is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.2, paragraph beginning "AI writing assistance also homogenised perceived writer personas"; details referred to SI:5.9, not in this PDF.

diversity_detail.metric: Standard deviation of perceived writer confidence ratings
diversity_detail.computed_over: Distributions of perceptions of human-written versus AI-assisted paragraphs across writers. The main text does not state whether ratings were first aggregated by paragraph or writer; the implementation is in unavailable SI:5.9 (p. 4, Section 2.2).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: The main text reports significant SD/entropy reductions for 22 of 29 attributes at p<.001 after Bonferroni correction. Attribute-specific tests, SEs/CIs, resampling method, and the independent unit used for uncertainty are not supplied in this PDF; see SI:5.9 (p. 4, Section 2.2).
diversity_detail.notes: Lower dispersion means less diversity. This is dispersion of reader perceptions elicited by writing, not embedding similarity or lexical overlap. The set unit describes the reported distributional summary; the underlying statistical unit cannot be verified without the supplement.

outcomes.name: Perceived paragraph originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded lay readers rate the paragraph on a 0-100 scale. Average marginal effects are from beta regressions, on the original rating scale, with reader random effects only; writer and proposition effects were omitted because of convergence problems. Unit is an individual reader rating, not a writer mean. The exact number of ratings in each fitted analysis is not stated. The full paragraph pool includes edited and unedited AI versions and is not the final analysis count. Robustness analyses excluding edits and model/input variants are referred to SI:5.6-5.8, absent here (pp. 5, 12-13, Figure 2 and Sections 4.6-4.7). Originality is explicitly shown in Figure 2B, although omitted from the markdown image conversion; no exact question wording is printed outside SI:2.4.

contrasts.reported: +12.5 pts more original for AI-assisted versus human writing; *** denotes p<.001 after Bonferroni correction across all 29 attributes. AME on the original 0-100 scale; no numeric SE, CI, arm means, or arm SDs for this outcome are printed.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Disclaimer content was randomized between writers: acceptable distortions, unacceptable distortions, both, or no disclaimer. All writers used AI; this was not randomized AI availability. Models/input formats were varied within writers as in Study 1. Disclaimer order within a message was also randomized (p. 13, Section 4.9).
assignment.quote: The content of the disclaimer was randomly assigned at the writer level across three disclaimer conditions and a no-disclaimer control.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/sf7rg (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: No disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance without the pop-up disclaimer; control count is not printed in the saved PDF and is not obtained by subtraction (p. 13, Section 4.9).

arms.name: Acceptable-distortions disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus warning about clearer and more relevant writing. Printed N=160 is treated as an analyzed/completer count, not an initial randomized count (p. 13, Section 4.9).

arms.name: Unacceptable-distortions disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus warning about more extreme views and less openness to change (p. 13, Section 4.9).

arms.name: Both-types disclaimer
arms.description: AI assistance plus all four distortion warnings (p. 13, Section 4.9).

participants.exclusions: 669 is the reported completed sample. Initial randomized counts and exclusions are not stated in this PDF; SI:1.4 holds attrition information (p. 11, Section 4.1).
participants.who: UK adults on Prolific; new writer sample, targeted census representativeness as in Study 1. No third-party rating panel was collected for this study (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.1 and 4.6).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o)
ai_tool.how_used: Structured drafting from the writer's stance rating or bullet points, or rewriting/improving the writer's own paragraph, followed by writer editing. Model/input pairings are randomized within writers in Studies 1 and 2. This is human use and editing of AI assistance, not an AI-only versus human-only output comparison. Models are accessed through OpenRouter (pp. 11-12, Sections 4.3-4.5).

task.description: Write political opinion paragraphs on three propositions sampled from a pool of 100. Writers first give a 0-100 stance rating, at least two explanatory bullet points, and their own paragraph of at least 100 words; they then edit an AI-generated paragraph until it reflects their opinion. AI paragraphs based on stance/bullets are requested at 100-150 words; paragraph-input conditions rewrite or improve the existing paragraph without changing its length (pp. 3, 11-12, Sections 2, 4.2, 4.4-4.5).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each writer experienced Prompting, Reranking, and No Intervention across their three propositions in random order. This supports a randomized within-person ai_design comparison. The writer's own unaided paragraph remains a preceding reference, not a randomized no-AI arm (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).
assignment.quote: Assignment was such that each writer, across the three propositions they were assigned, experienced all three conditions in random order, in a within-subjects design.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/sf7rg (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: No Intervention
arms.description: Default AI paragraph generation from writer bullet points; every writer experiences this and both mitigation configurations. No separately stated final arm-level writer count (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).

arms.name: Prompting
arms.description: Generation prompt adds instructions describing the polarizing distortion and asking AI to preserve writer stance (p. 14, Section 4.10).

arms.name: Reranking
arms.description: Reward models select the generated candidate predicted to minimize stance distortion relative to the writer's own text (p. 14, Section 4.10).

arms.name: Own paragraph (unaided reference)
arms.description: Writer-produced paragraph before AI generation, used as a reference for distortion; this baseline is not one of the three randomized AI configurations (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4 and 4.10).

participants.exclusions: 769 is the reported completed writer sample, not a stated initial randomized total. Initial assignment, attrition, and outcome-specific distinct writer counts are unavailable in the main PDF; attrition is in SI:1.4 (p. 11). No condition-specific participant losses are reported.
participants.who: New sample of UK adult writers recruited through Prolific with census-representative targets. A separate panel of 2,543 readers rated the paragraphs; 1,469 of those readers also took part in Study 1. Readers are not counted as writers assigned writing assistance (p. 11, Section 4.1).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o); GPT-4.1-based fine-tuned reward models for Reranking
ai_tool.how_used: AI supplies a paragraph from writer bullet points, followed by writer editing. Prompting instructs stance preservation. Reranking uses reward models trained on Study 1 data to predict paragraph stance and the stance implied by writer bullets and select a candidate. All three configurations still provide AI assistance (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.4, 4.5, 4.10).

task.description: Political opinion writing as in Study 1, with three propositions per writer; AI generation uses bullet-point inputs only. After generating a paragraph under the assigned mitigation configuration, writers can edit it. Separate blinded readers score the same 29 attributes, including originality, clarity, informativeness, relevance, and formality (pp. 7, 12-14, Sections 2.5, 4.4, 4.6, 4.10; attribute labels p. 5, Figure 2B).

outcomes.name: Perceived paragraph originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Study 3 collected blinded ratings on the same 29 attributes as Study 1, including originality and writing quality. Models use an intervention-condition regressor and reader random effects; the analysis unit is a reader rating. The printed reductions describe changes in AI-induced distortion relative to human writing, not standardized creativity effects or absolute arm means. Precise model outputs and additional contrasts are in unavailable SI:8.4. The paragraph pool of 5,016 is not a verified final per-outcome rating count (pp. 7, 12, 14, Sections 2.5, 4.6, 4.10). Originality is one of the writing-quality attributes shown in Figure 2B (p. 5). Study 3 rates the same attributes, but an identifiable originality effect, direction, SE, or CI for Reranking/Prompting versus No Intervention is not supplied in the main PDF. No direction is inferred from unlabeled points in Figure 4E.

studies.label: Study 4: Randomized reader exposure in a Trust Game

assignment.what_was_assigned: Readers received one paragraph from each source-type by distortion-level cell in random order. Randomization concerns exposure to existing writing, not assistance in producing writing. Source text includes human edits to AI paragraphs (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).
assignment.quote: Paragraph assignment was such that each Study 4 reader was assigned one paragraph from each cell in random order in a within-subjects design, without ever being assigned more than one paragraph per proposition.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 11, Methods: https://osf.io/38sg7 (registration reported by the paper; registry not independently opened).

arms.name: Human paragraph / low distortion
arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 human-written paragraph whose AI-assisted counterpart produced low persona distortion (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11). Readers receive no writing assistance.

arms.name: Human paragraph / high distortion
arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 human-written paragraph whose AI-assisted counterpart produced high distortion (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.name: AI-assisted paragraph / low distortion
arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 AI-assisted paragraph, including writer edits, with low distortion. The AI code describes the source text; no AI writing tool is assigned to this reader (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.name: AI-assisted paragraph / high distortion
arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 AI-assisted paragraph, including writer edits, with high distortion; reader exposure rather than writing assistance (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

participants.exclusions: 802 is the completed sample; initial randomized counts and exclusions are not stated in this PDF. Attrition is referred to SI:1.4 (p. 11).
participants.who: New UK adult reader sample recruited on Prolific; these are Trust Game decision-makers, not writers or the prior rating panel (pp. 11, 14-15, Sections 4.1 and 4.11).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o) generated the source paragraphs in Study 1; no AI tool used by the new readers
ai_tool.how_used: Existing human-written and AI-assisted paragraphs from Study 1 are shown to readers. This study does not assign a tool for producing new writing (pp. 14-15, Sections 4.11-4.12).

task.description: Read four existing paragraphs in randomized order and allocate part of a 20p endowment to each paragraph's author in a Trust Game. Source material comprises 800 Study 1 paragraphs, 200 per source-type by distortion cell. Primary outcome is allocation to the author, a measure of trust rather than creativity or diversity of newly produced output (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 human-written paragraph whose AI-assisted counterpart produced high distortion (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 AI-assisted paragraph, including writer edits, with low distortion. The AI code describes the source text; no AI writing tool is assigned to this reader (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.description: Exposure to an existing Study 1 AI-assisted paragraph, including writer edits, with high distortion; reader exposure rather than writing assistance (pp. 14-15, Section 4.11).

arms.name: Off-topic informational control
arms.description: An informational paragraph without a political stance (e.g. coral reefs or lighthouses); its authoring method is not stated. Coded other_aid to describe the active text exposure, not to infer how it was produced (p. 15, Section 4.12).

participants.exclusions: 7,996 is the completed sample; initial randomized counts and exclusions are not supplied in the main PDF. Attrition is referred to SI:1.4 (p. 11).
participants.who: New UK adult readers recruited on Prolific. These participants report political stance before and after paragraph exposure; they are not assigned writing assistance (pp. 11, 15, Sections 4.1 and 4.12).

ai_tool.name_model: Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek V3, and ChatGPT-4o (the ChatGPT version of GPT-4o) generated the source paragraphs in Study 1; no AI tool used by the new readers
ai_tool.how_used: Existing human-written and AI-assisted paragraphs from Study 1 are shown to readers. This study does not assign a tool for producing new writing (pp. 14-15, Sections 4.11-4.12).

task.description: Read five paragraphs and report stance before and after each on political propositions. Four paragraphs come from the same Study 1 subset used in Study 4 and one is off-topic control text. Primary outcome is the signed stance change toward the paragraph position, not creativity/diversity of output produced by these readers (p. 15, Section 4.12).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper's participants is stated. Within this paper, 1,469 Study 3 readers also participated in Study 1; writers are distinct across studies and separate from readers. Study 3 reward models reuse Study 1 training data. Studies 4 and 5 reuse Study 1 paragraph material, with new reader samples; their writer source corpus must not be treated as new independent writers.
sample_overlap.quote: 1,469 readers in Study 3 had previously participated as readers in Study 1 approximately five months earlier.

eligibility.reason: Study 3 meets all three criteria for ai_design: Prompting, Reranking, and No Intervention are delivered in randomized within-writer order (p. 13, Section 4.10); the reported completed writer sample is 769 people, excluding the rating panel (p. 11, Section 4.1); and blinded readers score the same 29 output/perception attributes as Study 1, including paragraph originality and writing quality (p. 7, Section 2.5; p. 12, Section 4.6; p. 14, Section 4.10; attribute labels p. 5, Figure 2B). Figure 4D also directly reports randomized effects on clarity, informativeness, and relevance (p. 8). Eligibility does not depend on a significant originality result, which is unavailable in the main PDF. Study 1 supplies observational context for fixed-order AI-versus-unaided writing and perceptual diversity (pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and Section 2.2); model/input randomization is not randomized AI availability. Study 2 has no third-party output ratings (p. 12, Section 4.6). Studies 4-5 manipulate reader exposure and measure trust/persuasion rather than new creative output (pp. 14-15).

one_line_finding: AI-assisted paragraphs were rated more original (+12.5 points; p. 5, Figure 2B) and showed lower dispersion on 22 of 29 perception attributes (p. 4, Section 2.2), while randomized reranking reduced the AI-induced clarity gain by 26.9% (p. 8, Figure 4D).
open_questions: Retrieve SI:8.4 for identifiable Study 3 originality contrasts, all configuration effects, numeric SEs/CIs, and outcome-specific analysis counts; the main PDF establishes measurement but not the originality result.
Retrieve SI:5.9 to establish the exact aggregation, dependence correction, and individual SD/entropy results. The 22-of-29 summary does not identify which unreported attributes changed.
Retrieve SI:1.4 for initial randomized/recruited totals, attrition, and distinct writer counts after output-based restrictions.
Reader-only random effects in the writing-rating models do not account for dependence by writer; assess writer-level precision before pooling (pp. 12-14, Sections 4.7 and 4.10).
SI:5.7-5.8 may support additional randomized model/input comparisons in Study 1; the coded AI-versus-unaided contrast itself remains non-randomized.
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. Read the entire markdown, including references, and checked PDF design/count/statistic pages. Figures 2 and 4 were also inspected as in-memory PDF renderings because their plotted labels are absent from extracted text; no image files were created. Originality in Figure 2B is an output rating and should not be lost by coding the paper solely as writer-persona perception. The paper explicitly contains five studies, not just the three writer studies in the abstract (p. 11). The form caps outcomes at 15: it retains five writing-output attributes in each of Studies 1 and 3 and five Study 1 dispersion attributes, prioritizing the printed confidence example and the core novelty/usefulness attributes. Remaining attribute-specific dispersion outcomes in SI:5.9 are omitted under the cap; all family-level numbers available in the main text are retained. Changes in inferred writer traits, demographic probabilities, political extremity, writer preferences/tolerance, edit rates, trust allocations, and reader political stance are not entered as creativity outcomes. Study 2 therefore has no coded outcomes; reader-exposure Studies 4-5 are coded other because their randomization does not assign writing assistance. Participant n_analyzed records the reported completed focal sample: writers in Studies 1-3 and behavioral reader participants in Studies 4-5. Separate writer-rating panels are described in who and are not added to intervention sample counts. Thus the largest focal study count is 7,996 in the out-of-scope persuasion study; the largest writer sample is 1,501, and the core randomized configuration study has 769 writers (p. 11). Initial randomized counts and final per-condition distinct-writer counts are left null where not printed; within-person arms must not be summed. The no-disclaimer count is not reconstructed by subtraction. n_units is null when a final analysis count is not reported; 10,008/5,016 paragraph pools and 2,903,596 total Study 1 ratings are not used as final per-outcome Ns (pp. 3, 12). No after_ai outcome is reported: unaided writing precedes AI exposure. Source-coded relative percentage reductions are not standardized effects. statistics_available does not assert regression_coefficient_se or complete arm statistics when the paper prints only an AME and significance; confidence dispersion has an empty availability list because the vocabulary has no category for SDs alone. No effect size, SE, arm count, or missing figure coordinate was calculated. Supplement/repository contents were not retrieved.
